report.label: Benchmark & field comparison — refreshed at fc3b875 (2026-08-05, shipped in v0.1.51)
report.supersedes: The July 2026 report this page used to cite. Its live-repo multipliers (36× tokens, and the older 20×) were measured against a build whose caller answers were a two-token placeholder — across 224 live answers it named zero callers. Those figures are retracted in full, not adjusted. The numbers here are smaller and they are real.

method.sampling: temperature 0 · 3 samples/cell · majority vote (threshold 2) · no tools
method.fixture: per language: a function `target`, exactly 15 direct callers c01–c15, 3 decoys n01–n03 — truth by construction

evidenceClasses.desc: a real model reads one context source and answers; the context is what is being measured, not the model
independent language-server ground truth on a real public repository
token / latency / build-time measurement, no accuracy claim attached

method.controlNote: `baseline` is a positive control — the raw fixture file, which contains the truth by construction, so its F1 of 1.000 confirms the judge works. It is a CEILING, not a competitor: Atlas does not beat it and does not claim to. `graphify` is the rival tool on the identical prompt and fixture.

headline.definition: tokens: sum of answer tokens over every query BOTH tools answered, across the 7-repo matrix. F1: deterministic set F1 of a real model's majority-voted caller list, given one context source, over 37 constructed-truth fixtures.

efficiency.controlNote: The raw-file control contains the answer by construction, so its F1 of 1.000 is a check that the judge works — a ceiling, not a competitor. Atlas does not beat it and does not claim to. The graph tool is the rival, on the identical prompt and fixture.

detailKnob.floorNote: Retrieval operations floor at high — an agent is never handed a truncated, and therefore wrong, caller list.

levels.note: not intended for caller retrieval — it scores 0.000 and the docs say so
same precision as high, lower recall
the default — the whole result at a tenth of xhigh's tokens
9.6× the tokens for an identical F1 — dominated by high

stats.label: Same F1, a tenth the cost

rows.evidence: unweighted mean of the 7 per-repo ratios
the floor, published because it is the floor
fixtures · 37 langs · mean context handed to the model
7 repos · median of 5 CLI runs each, spawn included
7 repos · warm daemon, per-repo mean of median explains

scorecard.note: Atlas is deterministic and LLM-free — the tool itself spends no tokens and never hallucinates. Only the agent reading its output spends tokens, and Atlas keeps that context small. Every ratio above is over queries BOTH tools answered; a query one tool missed is excluded rather than scored as a win.

retired.why: measured against a build that answered with a 2-token placeholder
same stub comparison; the honest figure is a same-host, same-run measurement
a percentage of an F1 is not a meaningful unit; the ratio and both raw values are published instead

retired.claim: 2.3× faster cold index / 14× faster incremental / 7.9× more call edges / 100.2% AST coverage
retired.why: not re-measured at this commit. A number nobody re-ran is not evidence.

report.fieldNote: Matching Atlas's coverage with the accurate alternatives means running 5 separate LSP servers or 4 separate SCIP indexers. They are precise by construction and serve as the accuracy reference — Atlas's aim is to match them as one fast multi-language tool. Against gopls call-hierarchy truth on a production Go service, Atlas measures F1 0.900 at this commit.
report.fieldCaveat: The index-time column above is carried from the July field survey and was NOT re-measured at this commit. It is a coverage-and-setup argument, not a performance claim, and no ratio on this page is computed from it.

latencyAtScale.why: Answering `who calls X` costs proportional to the number of callers returned, not the size of the codebase — indexing absorbs scale up front.
latencyAtScale.definition: warm-serve explain: per repo, the mean of that repo's four median `explain` responses against a warm daemon. The graph tool has no daemon mode, so this lane has no competitor and no ratio is claimed for it.

crossModel.note: The previous page showed the same fixtures scored by a second, larger model to argue the result is a property of the context rather than of one judge. That second lane was not re-run at this commit, so the comparison is withdrawn. The single-model caveat stands in its place: every F1 on this page is one model's majority vote over three samples at temperature 0.

limits: 5 of 37 fixture languages return no callers at this commit: ruby, pascal, razor, ejs and blade all score F1 0.000 on the constructed-truth fixture. Ruby's zero is by design — the fixture's callers are top-level, and the binder refuses to bind a top-level call rather than guess an owner. Pascal, razor, ejs and blade are genuine gaps. Ruby's L5 promotion rests on the LSP lane against a real repository, never on this fixture.

The competitor column is graphify 0.8.49. The previously published agent benchmark ran graphify 0.9.12, so part of the movement in that table is a version change on their side, not a change on ours. Both versions are named in the artifacts.

The Linux leg ran in an arm64 container on the Darwin workstation, not on the x86_64 host the published run used: no candidate Linux host accepted passwordless ssh, and the run rules forbid guessing a password. F1 is architecture-independent and stands; the Linux latency and index-time figures are NOT comparable to the published ones and are labelled accordingly.
The graph tool is not installed on the Linux leg, so that leg publishes no competitor ratio at all. The like-for-like comparison is the Darwin matrix.

The live-repo `serve` column was measured against the serve endpoint as it behaves at this commit, which still returns the reduced answer shape rather than the CLI's. Issue #144 is filed to bring serve to CLI parity in 0.1.51. Until it lands, the CLI column is the one to quote.
Two live repositories, byond and ets, show a WORSE token ratio than the retracted stub rows did. That is the retraction working as intended: the stub's larger number came from answering with nothing.

maturity.note: Levels reflect validation depth, not just support — an L2 language still indexes and searches; it simply has not reached verified call-graph resolution. A language moves DOWN when its evidence does: dart came off L5 this refresh.

levels.name: Reference-validated
levels.desc: call graph cross-checked against the language's own LSP server or a SCIP indexer, on a real public repository

levels.name: Real-repo call graph
levels.desc: who-calls resolved and proven on a real repository

fixtureOnly.evidence: F1 1.000 on the constructed-truth fixture at this commit (CALLERS_F1_AFTER.json). A fixture is a floor, not a promotion: these languages stay at L2 until a real-repo call-graph run lands.

fixtureGaps.badge: returns no callers on the fixture
fixtureGaps.evidence: F1 0.000 on the constructed-truth fixture at this commit — the caller list comes back empty.

retracted.why: July's dart PASS at .9249 rode a fan-out the truth filter should have refused. The verifier re-run measures .8631 against the same reference server on the same pinned repository. Dart returns to L4 until `toString`-scale fan-out and `package:` re-export families bind. We publish the retraction rather than the flattering number.

requalification.wasClaimed: native F1 1.000 each on the Linux saturation run
requalification.why: The saturation branch that produced that claim never merged. Re-measured at this commit, the fixture is perfect for 4 of the nine and returns an empty caller list for the rest. The site-wide fixture score is 32/37, not 37/37.
requalification.rubyNote: Ruby is a special case and is now L5 on LSP-truth (F1 1.000 against solargraph on rack, 9 symbols). Its 0.000 on the fixture is DESIGNED: the fixture's callers are top-level, and the binder refuses to attribute a top-level call to an owner it cannot prove rather than guessing one. Ruby's promotion cites the LSP lane and never the fixture.

definitions.token_ratio: sum(graphify answer tokens) / sum(atlas answer tokens) over that language's comparable queries
definitions.latency_ratio: sum(graphify ms) / sum(atlas ms) over the same queries; each ms is the median of 5 CLI invocations including process spawn

llmQa.label: Real-LLM caller-QA sweep — fc3b875, 2026-08-05 (shipped in v0.1.51)
llmQa.what: a real model is handed ONE context source and asked which functions call `target`; the answer is scored against the fixture's constructed truth. This measures the context, not the model.
llmQa.sampling: temperature 0 · 3 samples/cell · majority vote (threshold 2) · no tools
llmQa.prompt:
Using ONLY the context below, list the names of the functions that directly call `target`. Answer with ONLY a comma-separated list of function names, nothing else. If the context does not list caller names, answer with an empty line.

CONTEXT:
<context>

definitions.f1: deterministic set F1 of the majority-voted caller-name list against the fixture truth (15 callers, 3 decoys, truth by construction)
definitions.ctx_tokens: mean size of the context handed to the model, in tokens
definitions.controls: `baseline` is a positive control — the raw fixture file, which contains the truth by construction, so its F1 of 1.000 confirms the judge works. It is a CEILING, not a competitor: Atlas does not beat it and does not claim to. `graphify` is the rival tool on the identical prompt and fixture.

liveSummary.label: 36 live public repositories — fc68e26, 2026-08-05 (shipped in v0.1.51)
liveSummary.retraction: the `*_old` columns are the binary this page's previous live-repo multipliers were measured against. That build answered caller queries with a 2-token placeholder: across all 224 live answers it listed ZERO callers. Its ratios measured an empty answer, not a cheaper one, and are published here only so the retraction can be checked.
liveSummary.comparability: a query counts only when BOTH tools returned an answer; the stub column keeps its own comparability set because the stub answered where the current CLI sometimes declines

definitions.per_language_ratio: median(graphify tokens) / median(atlas tokens) over that language's comparable queries — a ratio of medians, robust to one runaway symbol
definitions.median_across_languages: the median of the 36 per-language ratios; each language counts once regardless of how many queries it contributed
definitions.pooled_sum: sum(graphify) / sum(atlas) over all comparable queries at once
definitions.per_query_median: the median of the per-query ratios across all comparable queries
definitions.cli: `atlas explain` run as a one-shot process, spawn included — what a shell loop or an agent shelling out actually pays
definitions.serve: the same query against a warm `atlas serve` daemon. NOTE: at this SHA the serve endpoint still returns the reduced answer shape; see the serve-parity note in the methods section

answerQuality.note: number of live answers that named at least one caller. The stub scored 0 of 224.

headline.definition: a language counts when its Atlas CLI answers named at least one caller across the run. On the excluded repositories Atlas returns a bare name or a name and a location, so the ratio measures a non-answer and is not published as a win.

excluded.why: the Atlas CLI named no caller on these repositories at this commit, so their token ratios describe the size difference between two non-answers. Several are large (lua 35.8×, rust 46.1×, terraform 38.5×) and every one of them is excluded from the headline for that reason.
excluded.note: Some of these are probe artefacts rather than binder gaps — byond's probes are markdown headings, rust's are type names — but the ratio is unusable either way, so the distinction does not rescue the number.

aggregatesAsMeasured.note: all 36 languages, including the 11 that named no caller. Published for completeness and for comparison with the retracted rows; NOT the headline.

vsStub.why_fell: the stub's larger ratio came from a two-token non-answer. The current CLI returns a real answer and therefore spends real tokens, so almost every honest multiplier is SMALLER than the one it replaces.
vsStub.why_rose: byond's ratio grew while still naming zero callers — a bigger multiplier for the same empty answer, which is why it is excluded from the headline. r's 274× is a single-language outlier on a detector-only comparison and is not representative of anything.

liveSummary.serveNote: The serve lane above was measured against the serve endpoint as it behaves at this commit, which still returns the reduced answer shape rather than the CLI's full one. Issue #144 is filed to bring serve to CLI parity in 0.1.51; until it lands, quote the CLI column.

supersedes.label: Agent-harness token benchmark — 2026-08-05 · Atlas 0.1.47-256-gfc68e26-dirty
supersedes.why: The gap narrowed. Atlas's F1 did not move (claude 0.995 → 0.995, codex 0.995 → 0.995). Two measured changes account for part of it: each harness's fixed floor rose (claude +5,173, codex +9,428 tokens), and a larger floor added to both sides pulls every ratio toward 1; and the newer codex is stronger without help (no-tool F1 0.831 → 0.941, 3.3 → 2.5 turns). Atlas's own per-question totals rose too (claude 58,234 → 76,205, codex 33,471 → 52,776); this run does not isolate why.

relevance.label: Natural-language relevance benchmark (#44) — 2026-10-29
relevance.buildNote: Measured on develop 3790ba95 plus the benchmark branch (atlas v0.1.52-700-g1a75deae (1a75deae, 2026-10-29T04:39:47Z)); no ranking code changed in the benchmark PR. Ships in 0.1.55.
relevance.what: 216 labelled questions over three frozen corpora, asked in natural language of three Atlas retrieval surfaces, each corpus indexed into a fresh store, scored offline against frozen labels — with a regression gate of 159 thresholds.
relevance.outOfScope: Chromium is out of scope for the gate: a Chromium index takes hours and tens of GB, which is a manual release check rather than a regression gate. The harness accepts any pinned corpus, so a Chromium entry can run as release validation.

labelSources.definition: mechanical — the LSP definitions recorded in the QA set
labelSources.callers: mechanical — the LSP caller names recorded in the QA set (matched by name)
labelSources.error_handling: hand-labelled from the code at the pinned commit; every item cites file:line
labelSources.adversarial: hand-written generic or stopword phrasings with no entity; the safe outcome is a refusal, or a grounded answer where the corpus has dedicated error machinery

surfaces.label: search, bare entity name (control)
surfaces.scored: results in order; the ticket's exact-search comparison

surfaces.label: context
surfaces.scored: symbols in emitted order, then unseen search hits

surfaces.label: code_query (MCP)
surfaces.invocation: MCP tools/call code_query {question, workspace, require_citations: true, detail: high}
surfaces.scored: citations in order; status insufficient is a refusal

gate.rule: each min = the measured develop baseline minus a margin, floored at 0: 0.03 pooled precision/MRR/recall/entity-first, 0.05 pooled refusal/safe, 0.06 per corpus, 0.09 per-corpus safe; every margin widened to one query's worth (1/n) for small sets. A missing metric fails closed.
gate.driftNote: Two back-to-back runs on fresh stores: 16 of 724 ranked lists differ, none at rank 1, gated drift 0 over all 159 thresholds (RESULTS.md, F8).
gate.catches: The gate catches regressions; it does not certify that retrieval is good — the baseline encodes today's defects, listed below as follow-ups. When a fix lands, the gate is re-frozen from a reviewed run so it ratchets.

relevance.holdsUp: Bare-identifier lookup works: the `search_exact` control puts the entity first in 71 of 76 cases (0.934). `code_query` routes `what calls <E>?` well: entity-first is 0.921 and query-word pollution is 0.013. Every definition is somewhere in the top 10 for 73 of 76 questions (R@10 0.961). On the clean, single-vocabulary C corpus, definition MRR is 0.97–1.00 on every surface. The trouble is in natural-language phrasing, mixed vocabularies and generic words, which is what the ticket reported.

findings.title: Question-template words are ranked as search terms (stopword pollution)
findings.status: open — proposed as a follow-up ticket
findings.proposed: "Lexical retrieval: drop question-template words from the BM25 query when the question also names an identifier." Acceptance: query-word top-1 ≤ 0.05 for definition and callers on all three surfaces.

findings.title: Entity-first routing exists for "what calls", not for "where is … defined"
findings.status: open — proposed as a follow-up ticket
findings.proposed: "Entity-first routing for where-defined and entity-scoped questions: a question token that is an exact indexed symbol name anchors that symbol at rank 1, as code_query already does for 'what calls'." Acceptance: definition entity-first ≥ the search_exact control on all surfaces, and error_handling MRR > 0 for Open/Append.

findings.title: A case-exact whole-name match does not outrank case-folded or partial matches
findings.status: open — proposed as a follow-up ticket
findings.proposed: "search: a case-exact whole-name symbol match ranks above case-folded and identifier-piece matches."

findings.title: Non-code facts outrank code for code-shaped questions
findings.status: open — proposed as a follow-up ticket
findings.proposed: "Config keys, workflow YAML and Makefile targets rank below code symbols for code-shaped questions, and `--corpus code` excludes file-level config facts." Acceptance: non-code@10 = 0 on definition and callers questions.

findings.title: search refuses real identifiers inside a question (false off-topic)
findings.status: open — proposed as a follow-up ticket
findings.proposed: "Off-topic guard: a query token that is an exact indexed symbol name qualifies the query as code." Acceptance: search callers empty rate 0.

findings.title: code_query's relevance floor (#60) grounds on generic words that happen to be symbol names, and keeps citations retrieved only by stopwords
findings.status: open — proposed as a follow-up ticket
findings.proposed: (a) "relevance floor: the exact_name rule ignores generic and stop words". (b) "relevance floor: prune lexical citations that match no query term". Acceptance: code_query adversarial safe ≥ 0.9.

findings.title: context never refuses and always ships a ~30 KB bundle

caveats: Callers labels are matched by name, which is the granularity of the LSP QA sets, so a same-named non-caller counts as a hit.
P@k for single-target definition questions is bounded by targets ÷ k. Read MRR and entity-first for those.
The error_handling and adversarial labels are one reviewer's reading of the code, with every item citing file:line.
Search callers recall (0.089) is low by design: search is lexical, not a graph walk. It is reported, not a defect.
Chromium (the ticket's large-repository corpus) is not in this gate. See README.md.

l5run.label: L4 → L5 promotion matrix — wave 2 verifier re-run, 2026-08-05 · macOS arm64
l5run.what: each candidate language's call graph cross-checked against ITS OWN language server on a real public repository — callHierarchy where the server offers it, references + documentSymbol enclosure otherwise. Deterministic set F1 on simple names. No LLM anywhere in the loop.
l5run.truth: per-language LSP reference server on a real public repository (callHierarchy preferred, references+documentSymbol enclosure fallback)
l5run.truthFilter: both sides restricted to textually-defined callers; macro/codegen-expanded caller names (no textual definition in the repo) excluded and listed per symbol
l5run.scoring: deterministic simple-name set comparison; no LLM
l5run.corroboration: where the two tools disagree, the source text adjudicates, and every excusal is listed per symbol. extras_reference_blind (all languages): an Atlas-only caller with a proven CALL SITE of the probe inside its own documentSymbol span is a reference-server blind spot, not a false positive. The site must be call-shaped in a spelling the language makes statically unambiguous (see corroboration_shapes) and must survive comment/string blanking — a name merely MENTIONED corroborates nothing. missed_reference_coarse (opt-in, see corroboration_languages): a truth-only caller whose body never mentions the probe in ANY shape — qualified, parenless, piped or captured — cannot be a textual call site, so it leaves the recall denominator (truth_scored) while truth_callers keeps the server's raw count. The two probes differ in strictness by design: crediting Atlas demands a proven call site, excusing Atlas is triggered by absence of evidence and so uses the widest possible net over the RAW text. A probe whose reference callers are ALL refuted measures nothing and is dropped from scoring and listed under unscorable_probes with both tools' answers.

rows.copy: Recovered at .9297/.9652 (fd vs rust-analyzer). July's published .9534 is RETRACTED: it depended on candidate order that the fail-closed binder no longer permits. Today's number is proven through `use`-declaration rungs.

Recovered at .9098/1.000 (monolog vs intelephense) — `use`-alias and namespace rungs bind cross-namespace static calls; every remaining miss is a listed cross-file test caller. July's 1.000 predated the fail-closed binder.
Canary held at .966/.9883 (Penlight vs lua-language-server) — one of the three no-regression canaries, unchanged all wave.

RETRACTED. July's published PASS at .9249 was unsound: it rode a fan-out the truth filter should have refused. The honest number is .8631 (precision .9723). Dart stays L4 until `toString`-scale fan-out and `package:` re-export families bind. We publish the retraction rather than the flattering number.
Canary held at 1.000/1.000 (json-fortran vs fortls, 8 symbols).
Canary held at 1.000/1.000 (zig-clap vs zls) — up from July's .9723.

Promoted at F1 1.000 / precision 1.000 (rack vs solargraph, 9 symbols) with zero adjudication excusals — the baseline's failures were all empty answers, fixed by binding implicit-self calls to their enclosing class. Ruby's separate 0.000 on the constructed fixture is a designed refusal, not a gap, and is never cited as evidence for this promotion.

Promoted at .9415/.9417 (swift-argument-parser vs sourcekit-lsp) — cross-file sends now bind through SwiftPM target membership; a same-name method family whose receiver cannot be proven stays unanswered rather than guessed.

Promoted at .9395/.9022 (ktlint vs kotlin-language-server) — a call reaches its package and its imports and nothing else: renamed-import decoys and cross-package bare calls refuse to bind. Thinnest margin in the set: precision clears the gate by .0022.

Promoted at 1.000/1.000 (plug vs elixir-ls) with truth-side corroboration ON and declared: elixir-ls attributes multi-clause calls to the public head, and every excusal is listed in the artifact and re-derivable from source. The same binary with corroboration off measures .7437 — both numbers are published.

Honest fail at .5533/.5667 (scopt vs Metals). Normalising Metals's val-attributed callers to their enclosing defs made the truth honest — and exposed that scopt's cross-file OParser builder chains are invisible to Atlas. The blocker is now named and measured rather than hidden by a flattering truth set.

l5run.carriedNote: 9 of the 20 languages in this matrix carry `carried: true` from the July base — they are outside the 11 wave-2 lanes and make no claim at this commit. They are listed rather than hidden, and none of them counts toward the reference-validated total.
l5run.reproduction: All 11 wave-2 lanes reproduced their claimed numbers to four decimal places on an independent verifier re-run, against a declared tolerance of |ΔF1|,|ΔP| ≤ .03 stated before the run. Every row carries its run timestamp and tree SHA.
l5run.honestyBracket: The elixir lane depends on truth-side adjudication, so it was re-run with that adjudication disabled: F1 .7437 / P .8403. Both numbers are published. The adjudication is worth exactly +.2563 F1 on that lane and every step of it is itemised per symbol in the artifact.
